title: The Nine Situations
hook: Two ward boards use different colors until Sophie gives both rivals one failing handoff.
counterintuition: Pressure does not have one correct leadership style. The useful move is to read the ground people are standing on and change conduct before unity becomes panic.
tryThisNow: Name your team's current ground, then change one leadership behavior to match it: persuasion for home ground, clarity for narrow ground, focus for desperate ground.
keyTakeaway: People change under different kinds of pressure; lead by matching conduct to the situation, using shared danger to create unity without manufacturing panic.

breakdown.fastRead:
Two ward boards use different colors after the merger notice. Sophie can give another speech about one hospital, or she can make the pressure real in a useful way. The patient transfer log shows one handoff neither ward can manage alone.

"They do not need another speech; they need the same storm," she says, pairing rival charge nurses on that handoff. The rivalry does not vanish. It becomes less important than the patient moving safely between systems.

The ground changes the people. Leadership begins by asking what kind of pressure they are under and what behavior that pressure now requires.
breakdown.deepRead:
Sam tapes the runway chart over the whiteboard at 1:30 in the morning. The cash balance gives the team six weeks, the regulatory checklist is incomplete, and three engineers are still bargaining for pet fixes. On dispersive ground, people drift toward home, comfort, and private preference. He removes side projects because the ground has changed.

Pressure must be named before it can be used.

The nine situations are not labels for memorization. Dispersive ground calls for restraint because people are close to home. Facile ground punishes lingering because the team has only stepped in lightly. Contentious ground is too valuable to attack blindly. Intersecting highways require allies. Serious ground calls for supplies and solidarity. Difficult ground asks for steady movement. Hemmed-in ground needs stratagem. Desperate ground requires action because delay becomes collapse.

A team under pressure should answer like the shuai-jan: touch one part and the whole body knows. The old image from the Ch'ang mountains is about responsiveness, not spectacle. If the head is struck, the tail answers. If the middle is struck, both ends know what to do.

Marquis Wu's tears belong beside his error: leadership has to count the lives that pay for bad ground. Grief after a bad decision does not repair the decision. The lesson is to read human pressure before people are spent by it.

The men of Wu and Yueh in the same boat show that shared danger can make old rivals pull with one rhythm.

The phrase the men of Wu and Yueh in the same boat is useful because danger gives opponents one shared surface to protect.
breakdown.fullRead:
When does closing the escape path create focus, and when does it create a body count? Vincent asks it at the warehouse door because chemical placards are stacked beside a single roll-up entrance. The entry tag board is clean, the thermal camera is working, and the exit rope runs straight. The building still gives the crew only one way out.

Desperate ground is powerful because it concentrates attention. It is also dangerous because the same concentration can become panic if the leader lies about the risk or traps people for pride. Vincent does not give a speech about courage. He sets the exit rope, limits the entry team, and names the stop condition before anyone crosses the threshold.

You cannot copy one leadership mood across every situation. On dispersive ground, people need a reason to stay with the mission. On intersecting highways, they need allies before argument hardens. On hemmed-in ground, they need a trick or a turn. On desperate ground, they need a visible line of action, not vague encouragement.

Loose gravel slides under Marit's lead truck at a mountain checkpoint. The clinic manifest is in the passenger seat, the checkpoint radio keeps cutting out, and the ally contact list is the only way around a stalled argument at the barrier. She treats the road as intersecting ground. Before anyone climbs down to argue, she calls two local partners who can keep medical supplies moving without turning the barrier into a contest of pride.

Shared danger can turn old rivals into two hands on the same oar. The men of Wu and Yueh in the same boat could hate each other on shore and still help each other crossing a river in a storm. The storm does not make them saints. It gives them one boat.

Warm air rolls from the walk-in freezer as Javier opens the kitchen door. The fish inventory is softening, the ice delivery is twenty minutes out, and the service clock is already running. His two sous-chefs have spent months guarding separate stations. He gives one the salvage list and the other the menu cuts, then makes them call changes to each other every five minutes. Head and tail now answer together.

It took Hiroshi one snapped sampling cable to stop managing departments and start managing the single boat they were all inside. The storm track had shifted, the sample freezer was near capacity, and the winch manual was open on the wet deck. Scientists blamed deck crew. Deck crew blamed the science schedule. After the cable snapped, he rebuilt the expedition around one shared sequence: secure the deck, save the samples, reset the winch, then decide whether to continue.

Use pressure cleanly. Do not invent crisis to get obedience. Do not keep people in false comfort when the ground has already changed. Tell the truth about the situation, remove distractions that belong to the old ground, and give people a shared action they can feel in their hands.

Shared danger can unify people, but honest leadership decides whether it steadies them or spends them.

examples.title: Sophie creates one handoff

planSpec.domain: hospital merger team integrating two rival wards
planSpec.audience: nursing director after a merger announcement
planSpec.stakes: old loyalties could fracture patient handoffs
planSpec.requiredBeat: They do not need another speech; they need the same storm, Sophie says, then pairs rival charge nurses on the one handoff neither ward can manage alone.

examples.scenario: "They do not need another speech; they need the same storm," Sophie says while two ward boards show different color codes. The merger notice is still fresh, the handoff checklist conflicts, and the patient transfer log shows one fragile transfer. Before rounds, she must decide whether to lecture about unity or give rival charge nurses one handoff neither ward can manage alone.
examples.whatToDo: Pair the rival charge nurses on the high-risk transfer and make the shared checklist visible. Let the patient need create one boat.
examples.whyItMatters: Old loyalty will not dissolve because management asks nicely. Shared danger, used honestly, can make cooperation practical before it becomes sentimental.

examples.title: Sam removes side quests

planSpec.domain: startup running out of runway before a regulatory deadline
planSpec.audience: founder with six weeks of cash
planSpec.stakes: panic could scatter engineers into pet fixes
planSpec.requiredBeat: At 1:30 a.m., Sam removes side projects from the board and makes the deadline visible enough that the team stops bargaining with dispersive ground.

examples.scenario: At 1:30 in the morning, Sam tapes the runway chart over a whiteboard crowded with side projects. The cash balance says six weeks, the regulatory checklist is incomplete, and feature freeze starts by noon. He has to choose whether to let engineers bargain for favorite fixes or make the ground visible enough that the team stops scattering.
examples.whatToDo: Remove side projects, post the cash balance and checklist, and turn the next six weeks into one visible sequence. Keep panic out by making focus concrete.
examples.whyItMatters: Dispersive ground lets private preference pull people apart. A real deadline, stated plainly, can concentrate work without faking crisis.

examples.title: Vincent limits the entry team

planSpec.domain: fire crew entering a warehouse with one exit route
planSpec.audience: incident commander at a chemical storage fire
planSpec.stakes: wrong pressure could trap firefighters inside
planSpec.requiredBeat: When does closing the escape path create focus, and when does it create a body count?

examples.scenario: When does closing the escape path create focus, and when does it create a body count? Vincent studies chemical placards beside a roll-up door. The entry tag board is ready, the thermal camera is charged, and the exit rope runs straight. Before the team enters, he must decide whether this is desperate ground that demands action or a trap that pride is trying to rename.
examples.whatToDo: Limit the entry team, set the exit rope, name the stop condition, and refuse any entry that depends on bravery replacing a second exit.
examples.whyItMatters: Desperate ground can focus people only when leadership is honest about risk. False pressure turns courage into casualties.

examples.title: Marit calls allies first

planSpec.domain: peacekeeping logistics team negotiating a mountain checkpoint
planSpec.stakes: a blocked road could isolate clinics for days
planSpec.requiredBeat: Loose gravel slides under the lead truck as Marit treats the checkpoint as intersecting ground and calls allies before anyone argues at the barrier.

examples.scenario: Loose gravel slides under the lead truck as Marit sees the mountain checkpoint ahead. The clinic manifest lists insulin and trauma kits, the checkpoint radio cuts out, and her ally contact list sits on the dashboard. Before anyone argues at the barrier, she has to decide whether this ground is a contest or an intersection that requires partners.
examples.whatToDo: Call the local allies before the convoy reaches the barrier. Use relationships to keep supplies moving instead of making the checkpoint a pride contest.
examples.whyItMatters: Intersecting ground belongs to the side that joins hands early. The right ally can change the road before the argument fixes it shut.

examples.title: Javier gives both rivals the salvage plan

planSpec.domain: professional kitchen after a freezer failure before service
planSpec.audience: executive chef with two rival sous-chefs
planSpec.stakes: the team can save service only if rivalry collapses into one response
planSpec.requiredBeat: Warm air rolls from the walk-in as Javier gives each rival half the salvage plan so head and tail answer together.

examples.scenario: In the restaurant walk-in before Saturday service, warm air rolls from the freezer while Javier checks the fish inventory. The ice delivery is late, the service clock keeps moving, and two rival sous-chefs are waiting to defend their stations. Before prep splits into blame, Javier must choose whether to manage personalities or make each rival hold half the salvage plan.
examples.whatToDo: Give one sous-chef the salvage inventory and the other the menu cuts, then require five-minute cross-calls until service stabilizes.
examples.whyItMatters: Pressure can make rivals useful if their tasks interlock. Head and tail respond together when neither side can finish alone.

examples.title: Hiroshi manages one boat

planSpec.domain: research vessel caught between storm and equipment failure
planSpec.audience: chief scientist leading a mixed crew
planSpec.stakes: scientists and deck crew must cooperate or lose the whole expedition
planSpec.requiredBeat: It took Hiroshi one snapped sampling cable to stop managing departments and start managing the single boat they were all inside.

examples.scenario: On the research vessel after a midnight squall, Hiroshi is the research lead who needed one snapped sampling cable to stop managing departments. The storm track shifted, the sample freezer was near capacity, and the winch manual lay open on a wet deck. After the failure, he had to decide how future storms would turn scientists and deck crew into one sequence instead of two offended groups.
examples.whatToDo: Build a single storm sequence: secure deck, preserve samples, reset the winch, and decide together whether the run continues.
examples.whyItMatters: Shared danger does not automatically create unity. It needs one visible order of action that makes every group part of the same boat.

questions.prompt: Two merged hospital wards keep separate routines, and a fragile patient transfer requires both systems to work together. What should the nursing director do first?
choices: Give a broad speech about teamwork.
Create one shared handoff that neither ward can complete alone.
Let each ward keep its own checklist until morale improves.
questions.explanation: The shared handoff creates honest common pressure. A speech stays abstract, while separate checklists leave old loyalty untouched.

questions.prompt: A startup has six weeks of cash and a regulatory deadline, but engineers keep defending favorite side projects. What leadership behavior fits the ground?
choices: Hide the cash balance to prevent anxiety.
Let every engineer keep one side project for morale.
Make the deadline visible and remove work that belongs to the old ground.
questions.explanation: The team is scattering on dispersive ground. Visible constraints and a feature freeze focus effort without inventing panic.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fire has one exit route. The entry team is brave, but chemicals and layout make withdrawal uncertain. What is the best evaluation?
choices: Limit entry, set a stop condition, and avoid turning pressure into a trap.
Send a larger crew because desperate ground always improves courage.
Block the exit rope so the team focuses completely.
questions.explanation: Desperate ground can concentrate action only when risk is honestly bounded. Blocking retreat for pride would create a body count, not unity.

questions.prompt: A medical convoy reaches a mountain checkpoint where local allies can influence the guards. What matches intersecting ground?
choices: Argue at the barrier to show resolve.
Call allies before the convoy turns the barrier into a public contest.
Split the convoy so each truck negotiates alone.
questions.explanation: Intersecting ground rewards joining hands early. Allies can change the road before the argument hardens.

questions.prompt: A freezer fails before dinner service, and two rival sous-chefs are ready to blame each other. How should the chef use the pressure?
choices: Give each rival an interlocking half of the salvage plan.
Send one rival home to avoid conflict.
Delay service until the rivalry is solved emotionally.
questions.explanation: Interlocking tasks make each rival part of one response. The pressure becomes useful because neither side can succeed alone.

questions.prompt: Scientists and deck crew on a research vessel blame each other after a cable snaps during a storm. What should the chief scientist change?
choices: Separate the groups so conflict cools naturally.
Create one storm sequence that links deck safety, samples, winch reset, and the continue-or-stop decision.
Let the department heads negotiate after the next sample run.
questions.explanation: Shared danger needs a shared order of action. A single sequence turns departments into one boat while the storm is still active.

questions.prompt: A team is still close to comfort and private preference, so people drift toward old routines whenever the work gets hard. What ground does this resemble?
choices: Dispersive ground.
Desperate ground.
Ground of intersecting highways.
questions.explanation: Dispersive ground pulls people back toward home or private interest. It calls for restraint and reasons to stay, not maximum pressure.

questions.prompt: A leader wants to create urgency by exaggerating a crisis, hoping that fear will make the team act as one. What is wrong with this?
choices: It may create obedience, but it spends trust and can turn pressure into panic.
It is always necessary because unity requires fear.
It fails only when the team is already too calm.
questions.explanation: Pressure must be truthful. Invented crisis may force motion, but it damages trust and makes later real danger harder to lead.

questions.prompt: A project reaches a point where delay will collapse the opportunity, and everyone can see the same irreversible deadline. What should leadership provide?
choices: Vague encouragement so people feel trusted.
A visible line of action that channels the pressure.
More optional work so people can choose their own path.
questions.explanation: Desperate ground needs action, not slogans. A visible sequence focuses courage and keeps pressure from scattering into panic.

reviewCards.front: A team is close to comfort and keeps drifting back. What ground should you recall?
reviewCards.back: Dispersive ground. People need a reason to stay with the mission before private preference takes over.

reviewCards.front: Rivals must cooperate because neither can solve the problem alone. What should you create?
reviewCards.back: Create one shared action with interlocking responsibilities. Shared danger can turn rivals into partners when the task is real.

reviewCards.front: A situation feels desperate. What separates useful focus from manipulation?
reviewCards.back: Truth. Name the real risk, set a line of action, and avoid manufacturing crisis for obedience.

reviewCards.front: A road depends on allies before a barrier hardens. What ground is this like?
reviewCards.back: Intersecting ground. Join hands early because partners can change the route before conflict fixes it shut.

reviewCards.front: Why does the shuai-jan image matter for teams?
reviewCards.back: It teaches responsive unity. When one part is touched, the rest knows how to answer without waiting for a separate speech.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to read the human pressure of a situation and change leadership conduct to fit it.

ifThenPlans.plan: If people drift toward private preferences, then I will make the real constraint visible and remove old-ground distractions.
If rival groups face one risk, then I will give them one interlocking task neither can complete alone.
If a situation looks desperate, then I will state the risk, set the stop condition, and give a visible sequence of action.
If a decision depends on a crossing point or gatekeeper, then I will call allies before the barrier becomes a pride contest.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Classify your team's current ground, then change one leadership behavior to match it. Remove one old-ground distraction or create one shared action.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: At the end of each week, review one tense moment and ask whether your conduct matched the ground people were actually standing on.

memorableLines.text: Pressure must be named before it can be used.
memorableLines.why: It makes urgency a diagnostic act rather than a mood.

memorableLines.text: Shared danger can turn old rivals into two hands on the same oar.
memorableLines.why: It lands the Wu and Yueh anchor as a modern leadership rule.

memorableLines.text: Shared danger can unify people, but honest leadership decides whether it steadies them or spends them.
memorableLines.why: It preserves the ethical limit on using pressure.
